title: Open WebUI changes agent defaults
summary: Open WebUI’s security update changes its database; optional tools need separate controls.

# Open WebUI changes agent defaults


By OpenTools Team


·


November 6, 2026


Back up before the migration; review changed tool defaults and choose computer‑access boundaries separately.


Open WebUI urges administrators to install[0.13.0](https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui/releases/tag/v0.13.0) for security fixes. Detailed advisories will follow CVE assignment, its release note says. The database migration needs preparation; computer access requires a separately configured Open Terminal connection for the Desktop and Browser tabs.


##


Back up before the cutover


Before changing versions, back up the database and associated files.[The update guide](https://docs.openwebui.com/getting-started/updating) says to stop every replica, let one migrate, then restart the others on the new version.` ENABLE_DB_MIGRATIONS=false` merely selects the migration runner; it cannot make a mixed‑version fleet safe.


A container‑tag rollback does not undo the migration: keep the pre‑update restore point. Preserve` WEBUI_SECRET_KEY` across container recreation or existing sessions are invalidated.


##


Check action defaults


The[walkthrough](https://openwebui.com/blog/v0-13-0-your-model-gets-a-computer) leaves sub‑agents off by default, but any enabled deployment needs concurrency, background, iteration and output caps; those now default to unlimited.


Native tool‑call rounds rise from 256 to 1,024 per response.` CHAT_RESPONSE_MAX_TOOL_CALL_ITERATIONS=256` restores the prior cap. Native‑calling models can create private Python tools for users allowed to create workspace tools; disable Tool Creation per model to prevent new tool creation.


Enable Tool Permissions before choosing Ask for approval; Full access runs tool calls immediately.


##


Choose the computer and shared session


[Open Terminal](https://docs.openwebui.com/features/open-terminal/) runs in Docker for isolation or directly on the host. Those are execution choices, distinct from the chat’s permissions.


A shared connection means shared files and running programs, even with a local model. Trusted‑team multi‑user workspaces differ from Enterprise‑licensed per‑user containers.


For uncontrolled sites, the[walkthrough](https://openwebui.com/blog/v0-13-0-your-model-gets-a-computer) recommends Docker, approvals and signing out: hostile page instructions can target local models too. Published Docker images disable Chromium’s own sandbox. Local inference keeps screenshots local; cloud inference sends them to the provider.


Choose the execution and sharing boundary before enabling optional actions. Approval prompts cannot replace a migration backup, and local inference does not establish per‑user isolation.
